note: Terms the report may use. The renderer prints only the terms that appear in the report. `match` lists the words that count as a use (lower case).

terms.meaning: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines: the international standard for accessible websites, published by the W3C. Version 2.2 is current.
WCAG requirements come in three levels. A is the minimum; AA is the level most laws and contracts refer to; AAA is the highest.
Software that reads the screen aloud, or shows it on a braille display, so people can use a website without seeing it.
A device that shows text as raised dots under the fingertips.
Software that enlarges part of the screen many times over.
Enlarging the whole page, for example with Ctrl and +.
Software that lets people click, type and scroll by speaking, for example by saying the words on a button.
One or two large buttons that step through items on screen, used by people with very limited movement.
The item the keyboard is on right now. Developers call it focus.
The visible outline that shows the keyboard position. Developers call it the focus indicator.
The text description of an image, read out by screen readers. Most content systems have a field for it.
On-screen text of what is said in a video, and of important sounds.
A narrated track that describes important visual details of a video.
The full text of a video or audio recording.
How much text or a shape stands out from its background, measured as a ratio such as 4.5:1. Higher is easier to see.
The unit web pages use for sizes. A phone screen is often about 320 to 400 pixels wide.
A window or panel that opens on top of the page, such as a cookie banner or a dialog. Developers call it a modal or dialog.
The text that says what a form field or button is for.
The name a screen reader or voice control uses for a button, link or field. Developers call it the accessible name.
A page element with no built-in meaning. Developers call it a div or span. Unlike a real button, software cannot tell what it does.
Parts of a page such as the header, menu and main content that screen readers can jump between. Developers call them landmarks.
Grey example text inside an empty form field. Developers call it a placeholder.
The area of a button or link that responds to a tap or click. Developers call it the target size.
A message that appears without reloading the page, such as "Added to cart".
A device setting that asks websites to limit animation.
Content from another site shown inside a page, such as a map, video player or payment form. Developers call it an iframe.
A group of pages built from the same layout, such as all product pages. A problem in the layout usually appears on every page of that type.
